comments.author: @jarrod752
comments.text: I like how you state Arizona's water problem is a _legal one_ when we're talking about independence. Arizona _could_ cut off California if they wanted to, but Nevada could also cut Arizona off, so you'd have 2 wolves and a lamb deciding what's for dinner. Also, Arizona cutting off California doesn't mean Arizona can immediately do anything useful, just stop it from flowing. The state could limp on for a year or 2 from the reservoirs, but that was only designed as a stopgap for temporary drought, not a permanent solution. I'd call Arizona doable if everybody honored the current water rights, rough but salvageable if Nevada didn't/couldn't cut off the Colorado, but Arizona cut off California (needing to rebuild infrastructure to pipe it from the north), and not possible otherwise without a much better water plan already in place for many years or another form of water independence.

replies.author: @GeographyEffect
replies.text: That’s a thoughtful way to frame it. Arizona’s problem isn’t simply that the water disappears, but that independence would turn an already fragile legal arrangement into a geopolitical one, while the physical infrastructure would still limit how quickly Arizona could adapt.

comments.text: Becoming an independent state does not require becoming an autarky (self-sufficiency without international trade). Some nationwide companies depend on offices in that state, so they will be crippled if a state responds to a US embargo by forbidding the office supply services across state lines. Texas, ERCOT, has spent the last 25 years overwhelmingly playing the Federal subsidy & tax credit game regarding new energy generation; as a result Texas has >40Gigawatts of installed wind capacity today compared to 181Megawatts in 2000.  This wind power is largely located in the Central Texas corridor anchored by Sweetwater where it has two disadvantages: 
a) relatively isolated (Fort Worth is the closest city of a million or more people, and its 190 miles from Sweetwater, Austin is 252 miles away), and 
b) the wind tends to blow most regularly overnight - i.e., in off-peak hours when its needed the least, and wind tends to subside to its diurnal nadir between 300 and 500pm the hottest part of the day in a Texas summer when it's needed the most.  PLUS the damn things FROZE during the severe events of Winter 2021 & 2023.
ERCOT has thus softened its grid by indulging i) in the pipe dream of inherently intermittent & unreliable power (and don't even get me started on the fact those things are NOT recyclable, and end up chopped up in unsightly boneyards awaiting a "final resting place" in overflowing landfills), while ii) enriching ranchers with hundreds of thousands of acres that just hold the world together otherwise good for only raising low-profit-margin cattle, and iii) allowing politicians to bloviate on the amount of "green" power in ERCOT.

Now that's the downside for Texas with ERCOT's quarter-century frolic & detour into "alternative" energy despite sitting atop more natural gas production than any other state.  That amount of natural gas production (from what some believe are massive reserves) is capable of firing highly-efficient 24/7/365 reliable combined cycle generation plants for centuries to come.  One can only hope the focus of ERCOT for the next quarter-century is focused on RELIABLES, not so-called "renewables."  Furthermore, the upside for Texas is found not simply in its US-leading crude oil & natural gas production, but more importantly in the fact that Texas is home to 
a) 33% of the US' refining capacity which turns all that crude oil into useful transportation fuels, and
b) 75% of the US' petrochemical processing capacity (that turns natural gas liquids - ethane, propane, butane, iso-butane and natural gasoline) into useful products which are inputs to nearly everything you touch on a daily basis.

And with the political will behind it, Boston's public transportation could be expanded to the point that cars are no longer necessary for state residences, an infrastructure project that would surely become a priority in a situation where every drop of gasoline represents a reduction in the country of Massachusetts's wealth. Food is plentiful thanks to amble fishing grounds and robust farming in the western portion of the state around the Connecticut River Valley (some of the richest soils in North America!). The main issues holding Massachusetts back as an independent state come down to lack of infrastructure, which again is a political problem and not a physical one. Young people leave the state due to lack of mid range housing, and the transportation connections across the state are outdated and focused on cars, which are not sustainable long term if Massachusetts were cut off from the rest of the United States and easy supplies of gasoline. With a leadership focused on independence and by following the likes of countries like Singapore and The Netherlands - investment in renewables, ease of access to public transport, fair housing, regenerative farming, high levels of education and the associated high tech industries, and perhaps an expansion on nascent industries like mollusk and seaweed farming, Massachusetts would easily grow to become a powerful, dynamic country.

replies.author: @GeographyEffect
replies.text: That’s a thoughtful case for Massachusetts, especially the distinction between physical limits and infrastructure choices. My ranking was weighted toward what each state could rely on immediately, but over time investment, human capital, and adaptation could change the picture substantially.
